title: Habakkuk
summary: Habakkuk is a biblical book focused on justice, faith, lament, and hope under imperial threat.
historical_context: Habakkuk brings hard questions about violence and judgment before God and ends in faithful worship.
ancient_near_east_context: Habakkuk belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Habakkuk should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Habakkuk as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 8 of 12, Habakkuk contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting justice, faith, lament, and hope under imperial threat to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Habakkuk as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Habakkuk uses prophecy, poetry within Minor Prophets, book 8 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Habakkuk helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Habakkuk anchors justice, faith, lament, and hope under imperial threat within Minor Prophets, book 8 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

related_objects.notes: Babylon forms the looming imperial crisis.
The book wrestles with God's justice amid violence.
The righteous live by faith amid unanswered questions.
Judgment language addresses Judah and the nations.
The closing prayer models hope in crisis.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Habakkuk first within its own literary setting before moving to broader canonical connections.
